title: Mahershala Ali Says Two Oscars Have Not Solved Hollywood's Shortage of Roles
excerpt:
The Moonlight and Green Book actor says awards do not guarantee access to strong scripts.
He argues that many greenlit projects simply contain no suitable part for him.
body_md:
Mahershala Ali has won two Academy Awards, yet he says the industry's highest acting recognition does not automatically translate into a steady supply of compelling roles. In a conversation on the 7PM in Brooklyn podcast with Carmelo Anthony and Kazeem Famuyide, the actor described the structural limitations that remain even after major career milestones.

Ali won supporting actor Oscars for Moonlight and Green Book. Those achievements established him as one of the most decorated performers of his generation, but he argues that awards cannot create parts that have never been written. There are more talented actors than strong projects, he explained, and only a relatively small portion of produced material offers the right combination of character, story, and opportunity.

His concern goes beyond ordinary competition at auditions. Ali said that many projects receiving production approval do not include a suitable role for him at all. Even a performer with numerous awards would still be waiting if writers and decision-makers were not developing material with a broader range of people and experiences in mind.

He also addressed the potential consequences of reduced diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives. Ali did not claim to know the exact scale of their impact, but suggested that institutional priorities influence which stories receive funding. Without an incentive to reflect the world outside their offices, he argued, executives may continue to center the perspectives already most familiar to them.

Producing original material is one possible response, though Ali emphasized how difficult that route can be. Developing a project from concept to screen may take years, which means creating opportunities independently is not an instant solution for working actors.

The actor also questioned the idea that a Black performer becomes fully validated only after winning an Oscar. Symbolic recognition matters, but he said it has limited practical value if it does not lead to meaningful work. He does not want to be defined by a token diversity assignment; he wants the chance to contribute to strong stories as an artist and individual.

Ali's comments reveal a distinction that award-season narratives can obscure. A celebrated performance may earn prestige and visibility, but decisions about what gets written, financed, and produced ultimately determine which roles exist. His experience suggests that individual success does not necessarily remove broader barriers within the film industry.
seo_title: Mahershala Ali on Why Two Oscars Do Not Guarantee Roles
seo_description: Mahershala Ali discusses the scarcity of suitable roles, the limits of Oscar recognition, and Hollywood's greenlighting decisions.
